title: Detection of Phishing for Information
summary: This detection strategy covers phishing for information, the technique where an adversary sends a message that asks the target to reveal something, such as credentials, a multifactor code, a virtual private network configuration or details of internal systems, without deploying any malicious code. It matters because the message needs no attachment and no exploit, so endpoint protection has nothing to block, and the only remaining signals are mail gateway metadata, message authentication results, link and domain characteristics, user click telemetry and help desk reports of unusual requests. The telemetry that makes it possible is mail gateway and cloud mail audit logs with sender, reply to address, authentication results and link destinations, secure web gateway records of visits to credential pages, identity provider logs of failed credential entry followed by a successful one, and help desk ticket records. Detection fails because a single well written message to one employee matches none of the bulk signals a rule relies on.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for messages that ask for information instead of carrying a file. The attacker wants your password, a login code or details about your systems. The rule watches mail metadata, the links in the message and whether anyone clicked. It also watches unusual requests to the help desk.
beginner.whyItMatters: There is no file to scan, so antivirus tools stay quiet. A good message can fool a careful person, because it asks for something the job already involves. If the person answers, the attacker has a real account. Finding the message in flight stops the attack before anyone replies.
howItWorks: The mail gateway records the sender, the reply to address, the authentication results and every link in the message.
Cloud mail audit logs record where the message was delivered and whether it was read or reported.
The web gateway records any visit to a linked page, including a page that asks for a password.
The identity provider records several failed sign in attempts for a real account from an unusual address.
The rule joins the message, the click and the failed sign in attempts within one short window.
A confirmed chain raises an alert, and the recipient is contacted to reset the password and report the message.
beginner.example: Think of a receptionist who receives a phone call from someone claiming to be the telephone engineer. The caller asks for the alarm code to test the line. No door is forced and no bag is taken. The request itself is the attack. This detection listens for the call.
takeaways: Phishing for information carries no malware, so mail metadata is the main evidence.
A click plus a run of failed sign ins is the strongest confirmation chain.
Train staff to report the request, not only the link.

objectives: Explain how phishing for information differs from phishing that delivers malware.
Identify the mail gateway, proxy and identity fields needed to detect this activity.
Write a correlation rule that links a message, a click and failed authentication.
Describe how help desk and reporting workflows create useful detection data.
Explain the response steps that limit damage after a user reveals information.
dataSources: Mail gateway logs with sender address, reply to address, message authentication results and embedded uniform resource locators
Cloud mail audit logs recording delivery, read status and user reported message events
Secure web gateway logs showing which user opened a campaign link and which credential page was displayed
Identity provider sign in logs showing repeated failed attempts followed by a success for the same account
Help desk ticketing records for unusual requests such as password resets, code sharing or remote access setup
logic: The pattern is an inbound message whose authentication results show a failed or missing sender policy check, whose reply to address differs from the sender, and whose link leads to a page that requests credentials, followed within minutes by a click from a corporate address and then by failed sign in attempts using the account that clicked. The fields that must be correlated are the sender and reply to domains, the authentication results, the link destination, the recipient and the click time, the authentication attempts and their source addresses, and the ticket or report trail. The benign case is a legitimate supplier whose mail fails authentication after a mailing platform change, sending users to a password protected portal where they mistype a password; the malicious case is a short window in which several users receive the same lure, at least one clicks, and authentication attempts for that account come from an unfamiliar hosting address.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Credential Lure Click Followed by Failed Authentication
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   service: mail_gateway
# detection:
#   selection_mail:
#     direction: 'inbound'
#     auth_result|contains: 'fail'
#     reply_to_domain: 'free-mail-example'
#   selection_click:
#     url_category: 'credential-harvest'
#   condition: selection_mail and selection_click | count() by recipient > 1 within 1h
# level: high
falsePositives: A legitimate supplier whose mailing platform is misconfigured and sends users to a password protected customer portal
Password expiry notifications from an internal system that use a link and a different reply to address
A conference or webinar platform that sends a sign in link and then receives mistyped passwords
An employee who forwards a genuine message to a personal address and then mistypes the password on a new device
tuningNotes: Start with authentication failure and reply to mismatch as the two required mail conditions, then add the click or the failed sign in as the confirmation signal so that ordinary misconfigured supplier mail does not page anyone. Allow list the mailing platforms and portals of regular suppliers and review that list monthly. Scope the high severity rule to finance, executive and privileged administrator mailboxes, and keep a low severity feed across all mailboxes for trend review. Correlating on clicks means a user who reads the message and phones the help desk instead is invisible, so also alert on help desk tickets that describe a password or code request.
